intro: This unit introduces Michael S. Heiser (1963–2023). He was a scholar who read the Hebrew Bible in its first language. He also read other old languages, like Greek and Ugaritic. His big idea was to read the Bible the way its first readers did.

You will meet the Hebrew word elohim. Heiser said it names beings whose home is the spirit world. Then you will read the Bible's council scenes. They are in Psalm 82, Psalm 89, 1 Kings 22, Job 1–2 and Isaiah 6. Heiser called this picture the divine council, God's heavenly court.

Readers do not all agree about these passages. You will learn Heiser's reading and at least one other reading. By the end, you will be able to explain a passage, name who said what, and compare two readings fairly.
bigQuestion: What did Michael Heiser notice about God's heavenly council, and how do other readers see the same passages?

timeline.t: Scribes at Ugarit write clay tablets about the god El and his assembly
Isaiah 6 tells of Isaiah's vision in the year King Uzziah died
The King James Version of the Bible is published in English
A farmer in Syria uncovers a tomb that leads to the ruins of Ugarit
Diggers begin finding thousands of clay tablets at Ugarit
Heiser earns his PhD at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, writing on the divine council
Heiser begins the Naked Bible Podcast
Heiser publishes The Unseen Realm and Supernatural
Heiser dies; his books and podcast are still read and heard

words.d: a person who studies one subject very deeply and writes about it
the books Jewish readers call the Tanakh and Christians call the Old Testament
the language of the old city of Ugarit in Syria, a close cousin of Hebrew
the time, place and ideas around a text that help explain what it means
a Hebrew word used for Israel's God and also for other beings of the spirit world
one of a kind; Heiser said no other elohim is like Israel's God
a gathering of heavenly beings with God at the head, like a king's court
a phrase the Hebrew Bible uses for heavenly beings in God's council
a Bible phrase for the many heavenly beings around God's throne
a Hebrew title in Job meaning the adversary, a member who challenges before God
heavenly beings with six wings in Isaiah 6; the name may mean burning ones
a reader's explanation of what a text means

choices: A scholar of the Hebrew Bible and ancient languages
test.why: Heiser (1963–2023) was a scholar of the Hebrew Bible and Semitic languages.

test.q: What was the subject of Heiser's 2004 dissertation?
test.why: His dissertation studied the divine council in ancient Jewish writings.

test.q: Which 2015 book is Heiser's shorter, easier telling of his main ideas?
test.why: Supernatural (2015) presents the ideas of The Unseen Realm more simply.

test.q: Why did Heiser read Ugaritic texts?
choices: They are part of the New Testament
They use words and ideas the Bible's neighbors knew
test.why: Ugaritic is a cousin of Hebrew, and its tablets show ideas the Bible's first readers' neighbors knew.

test.q: What was Heiser's big idea about reading the Bible?
choices: Read it only in modern translations
Read it as a science book
Read it without looking at words
Read it in its own context, like its first readers
test.why: Heiser urged reading the Bible the way its first readers understood it.

test.q: Heiser said the word elohim tells you what about a being?
choices: That its home is the spirit world
That it is equal to God
That it is a human judge
test.why: Heiser described elohim as a word about residence, not about what a being is like.

test.q: How do Hebrew readers know if elohim means one being or many?
choices: From the color of the ink
From the words around it, like the verb
test.why: Context, such as a verb for one person, shows whether elohim means one or many.

test.q: Which verse asks who among the gods is like the LORD?
test.why: Exodus 15:11, in the song after crossing the sea, asks this question.

test.q: In Psalm 82, what does God judge the council members for?
choices: Judging unfairly and not protecting the weak
test.why: Psalm 82:2–4 says they judged unfairly and did not protect the poor and weak.

test.q: Who saw the LORD on his throne with the host of heaven on his right and left?
test.why: The prophet Micaiah describes this vision in 1 Kings 22:19.

test.q: In Isaiah 6:8, God asks, 'Who will go for us?' How did Heiser read the word us?
choices: As Isaiah speaking to his friends
As God speaking to his council
As the seraphim speaking to Isaiah
test.why: Heiser read the us as God addressing the divine council; other readers see it differently.

test.q: What does the Hebrew word satan mean in Job 1–2?
test.why: Satan means adversary; in Job it appears as a title, the satan.

test.q: Which reading of Psalm 82 did John Calvin hold?
choices: The gods are human rulers and judges
test.why: Calvin read the gods of Psalm 82 as human rulers and judges.

test.q: Why did Heiser say Psalm 82:7 points to heavenly beings?
choices: Telling humans they will die like humans would be odd
test.why: Heiser argued 'you will die like humans' makes most sense if the listeners are not human.

test.q: Which New Testament verse quotes Psalm 82:6?
test.why: In John 10:34 Jesus quotes 'I said, Ye are gods' from Psalm 82:6.

write.prompt: Who are the gods in Psalm 82? Use Psalm 82:1 and 82:6–8 and one more passage from this unit, like Psalm 89:5–7 or John 10:34–35. Explain what the texts say, what Heiser argued, and how other readers see it.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse each time you use a passage.
Say who holds each view: Heiser argued, some readers say.
Use unit words like elohim and divine council, and explain them.
Compare the two readings fairly; show the clues each one uses.
